newsitem.title: JAPAN: Risk of yen's hard landing haunts forex market.
newsitem.headline: Risk of yen's hard landing haunts forex market.

text.p: Talk of a "hard landing" for the Japanese yen is surfacing in the foreign exchange market, where pent-up demand to sell the currency is gaining strength and raising concerns about where it may end, senior traders say.
Some market watchers say the yen's slide mirrors the outflow of capital as investors look for higher yields abroad.
"This trend is unlikely to be reversed anytime soon given continuing interest in unloading the currency," said Yukuo Takahashi, managing director of Chase Manhattan Bank's Global Trading Division.
The dollar hit a new 42-month high of 114.92 in Tokyo on Tuesday, marking a 44 percent retracement from its historical low of 79.75 yen set on April 19, 1995.
Traders say that small investors are playing a big role in the process of the yen's fall.

Faced with a lack of attractive investment vehicles at home, Japanese investor holdings in foreign currency bonds and deposits are expected to top 10 trillion yen ($87.7 billion) by the end of 1996, up 70 percent from a year ago.
There is also heavy demand for foreign currency from globe-trotting Japanese who spent 1.68 trillion yen ($14.7 billion) more than foreign tourists in Japan in the first half of the year.

Chase's Takahashi said that yen sales by small investors alone more than offset the nation's current account trade surplus, which totalled 3.61 trillion yen ($31.6 billion) in the first six months of the calendar year.
And the outflows may worsen since major institutions still have cash allocated to overseas investments.

"We have so far used only a part of funds earmarked for purchases of foreign bonds in the second half the current fiscal year," said Rikio Nagahama, chief general manager of securities investment at Dai-Ichi Mutual Life Insurance Co.

He told Reuters that the company bought approximately 100 billion yen ($877 million) worth of foreign bonds, mostly U.S. and German debt, in the April-September period and has similar plans for the six months ending March 1997.
Major capital outflow of the yen into foreign currencies is also apparent in the primary yen bond market.

"The yen is becoming the world funding currency. This implies a further weakening of the yen because foreign issuers convert all the yen-based funds into other currencies of their choice," said a senior brokerage trader.
Non-residents of Japan issued a record 11.52 trillion yen ($101 billion) in Euroyen bonds in 1995/96 to March 31, compared with 10.86 trillion yen ($95.2 billion) a year ago.
With Japan's official discount rate at a record low of 0.5 percent since September 1995, analysts predict that 1996/97 will be another record year.
Analysts say that none of the trends show any sign of reversal, suggesting that the fall in the yen may steepen dramatically. -- Tokyo Treasury Desk 813-3432-8676
